name: 2-Link Arm End-Effector X
description: Computes the horizontal (X) position of a planar two-link arm's end-effector as l1·cos(a) plus l2·cos(a+b), the sum of the two link projections onto the X axis. It is the forward-kinematics X coordinate from the joint angles.
notes: Joint angles are in radians, with a measured from the base and b relative to the first link. Coordinates are relative to the shoulder joint; the result shares the length unit of the links.

name: 2-Link Arm End-Effector Y
description: Computes the vertical (Y) position of a planar two-link arm's end-effector as l1·sin(a) plus l2·sin(a+b), the sum of the two link projections onto the Y axis. It completes the forward-kinematics coordinate pair.
notes: Joint angles are in radians, with b measured relative to the first link. Position is referenced to the shoulder joint and shares the links' length unit.

name: 2-Link Arm Reach (Elbow Angle)
description: Gives the straight-line reach from shoulder to end-effector for a two-link arm at a given elbow angle, from the law of cosines: sqrt(l1² + l2² + 2·l1·l2·cos(b)). It is the distance the tip sits from the base.
notes: The elbow angle b is in radians; b = 0 gives the fully extended reach l1 + l2. Because the plus sign is used, b here is the angle between the links' forward directions.

name: 2-Link Arm Elbow Angle (Inverse Kinematics)
description: Solves the inverse kinematics for the elbow angle of a two-link arm reaching target (x, y), using arccos of (x² + y² − l1² − l2²) divided by 2·l1·l2. It returns the joint bend needed to place the tip at the target.
notes: The target must be reachable, so |l1 − l2| ≤ distance ≤ l1 + l2, or the arccos argument leaves the valid range. The result gives one of two mirror solutions (elbow-up or elbow-down); angle is in radians.

name: 2-Link Arm Workspace Area
description: Estimates the reachable workspace area of a two-link planar arm as 4·pi·l1·l2. This is the area of the annulus between the maximum reach (l1 + l2) and minimum reach (|l1 − l2|) circles.
notes: The formula assumes full 360° joint rotation with no obstacles or joint limits; real workspaces are smaller. It equals the annular area only, not counting orientation reachability.

name: 2-Link Arm Manipulability Measure
description: Computes a two-link arm's manipulability measure as l1·l2·|sin(b)|, the magnitude of the Jacobian determinant. It quantifies how easily the end-effector can move in all directions at a given elbow angle.
notes: The elbow angle b is in radians; manipulability peaks near b = pi/2 and drops to zero at full extension or folding, where the arm is singular. It is a relative dexterity index, not a physical area despite the units.

name: Differential Drive Linear Velocity
description: Computes the forward linear velocity of a differential-drive robot as the wheel radius times the average of the left and right wheel angular speeds, rw·(wl + wr)/2. It gives the speed of the robot's centre point.
notes: Wheel angular speeds are in radians per second and radius in metres, giving metres per second. Assumes rolling without slip; equal wheel speeds produce pure straight-line motion.

name: Differential Drive Angular Velocity
description: Gives the yaw (turning) angular velocity of a differential-drive robot as wheel radius times the difference of right and left wheel angular speeds, divided by the wheel track, rw·(wr − wl)/L. It describes how fast the robot rotates about its centre.
notes: Wheel track L is the distance between the two wheels; wheel speeds are in radians per second. A positive result means turning toward the slower (left) wheel; equal speeds give zero rotation.

name: Differential Drive Instantaneous Turning Radius
description: Computes the instantaneous turning radius of a differential-drive robot as half the wheel track times the sum of the wheel speeds divided by their difference, (L/2)·(wr + wl)/(wr − wl). It locates the centre about which the robot is momentarily rotating.
notes: Wheel track L is the spacing between wheels; equal wheel speeds make the denominator zero, meaning an infinite (straight-line) radius. The sign indicates which side of the robot the turn centre lies on.

name: Wheel Odometry Distance
description: Computes the linear distance a wheel has travelled from encoder counts, as the wheel circumference 2·pi·rw times ticks divided by ticks per revolution N. It converts encoder pulses into travelled distance.
notes: N is the encoder counts per full wheel revolution; ticks and N are dimensionless counts. Assumes no wheel slip, so accumulated slip causes odometry drift over distance.

name: Wheel Speed from Encoder Frequency
description: Computes wheel surface speed from encoder pulse frequency as the wheel circumference 2·pi·rw times pulse frequency divided by (counts per revolution times quadrature factor), giving metres per second. It turns a real-time pulse rate into linear speed.
notes: N·q is the effective counts per revolution after quadrature decoding; frequency is in hertz. Assumes no slip, and q is typically 4 for full quadrature counting.

name: Quadrature Encoder Resolution
description: Gives the angular resolution of a quadrature encoder in degrees, 360 divided by (counts per revolution times quadrature factor). It is the smallest shaft angle change that the encoder can distinguish.
notes: Quadrature decoding multiplies base counts by q (usually 4), so N·q is the effective resolution. Counts and factor are dimensionless; a smaller result means finer angular precision.

name: Stepper Motor Step Angle (Microstepping)
description: Computes the effective step angle of a stepper motor under microstepping as 360 divided by (full steps per revolution times microstep divisor). It gives the shaft rotation per microstep in degrees.
notes: Both inputs are dimensionless counts; a higher microstep divisor gives finer angular steps but less torque per step. Actual positioning accuracy may be worse than the theoretical step due to microstep error.

name: Stepper Leadscrew Linear Resolution
description: Gives the linear travel per microstep of a leadscrew driven by a stepper motor, as the screw lead divided by (full steps per revolution times microstep divisor). It is the smallest commandable linear increment.
notes: Screw lead is the axial advance per full revolution (in millimetres here), so the result is in millimetres. Backlash and mechanical error can make real resolution coarser than this ideal value.

name: Gearbox Output Speed
description: Computes the output shaft speed of a reduction gearbox as the input speed divided by the gear reduction ratio. A higher ratio produces proportionally slower output rotation.
notes: Input and output speeds share the same unit (rpm here); the gear ratio is dimensionless. This is the ideal kinematic relation and does not account for slip or backlash.

name: Gearbox Output Torque (with Efficiency)
description: Gives the output torque of a reduction gearbox as input torque times the gear reduction ratio times efficiency. The ratio multiplies torque while efficiency accounts for frictional losses.
notes: Efficiency is a fraction between 0 and 1; input and output torque share the same unit. Torque is multiplied by the ratio even though speed is divided by it, conserving power minus losses.

name: Reflected Load Inertia (Gearbox)
description: Computes the load inertia as seen at the motor shaft through a gearbox, the load inertia divided by the square of the gear ratio. Reduction gearing sharply lowers the inertia the motor must accelerate.
notes: The ratio is squared because both speed and torque scale with it, so a ratio of 50 divides reflected inertia by 2500. Load and reflected inertia share units (kg·m^2); this ignores the gearbox's own inertia.

name: Payload Rotational Inertia (Point Mass)
description: Computes the rotational (moment of) inertia of a payload treated as a point mass, as mass times the square of its distance from the rotation axis, m·r². It quantifies resistance to angular acceleration about that axis.
notes: Valid only when the payload size is small compared with r, so it can be idealised as a point. Distance is measured perpendicular to the axis; result is in kg·m^2 and grows with the square of r.

name: Motor Torque for Angular Acceleration and Friction
description: Computes the motor torque needed to drive a rotating load as inertia times angular acceleration plus viscous damping times angular speed, J·alpha + bd·w. It sums the torque to accelerate the inertia and the torque to overcome speed-proportional friction.
notes: Angular acceleration is in rad/s^2 and speed in rad/s; the damping term scales with speed, not acceleration. It omits static friction, gravity and load torque, which may add further demand.

name: DC Motor Angular Speed (Back-EMF)
description: Estimates the no-load-corrected rotational speed of a brushed DC motor. It subtracts the resistive voltage drop I×R from the terminal voltage to get the back-EMF, then divides by the back-EMF constant Ke to yield the shaft speed in radians per second.
notes: Assumes a linear motor model at steady state; Ke here is in V·s/rad, so the result is angular speed. Divide by 2π/60 to convert to rpm. Ignores brush drop and magnetic saturation.

name: DC Motor Torque Constant Relation
description: Calculates the mechanical torque produced by a DC motor as the product of its torque constant Kt and the armature current I. The output is the shaft torque in newton-metres for the given operating current.
notes: Valid in the linear region below magnetic saturation. In SI units the torque constant Kt (N·m/A) equals the back-EMF constant Ke (V·s/rad) numerically. Uses actual current, not rated current.

name: DC Motor Stall Torque
description: Estimates the maximum (stall) torque of a DC motor when the rotor is held stationary. With zero speed there is no back-EMF, so the current is limited only by winding resistance to V/R, and torque is Kt×V/R.
notes: Represents the theoretical peak torque; the resulting stall current V/R can be very large and may damage the motor or supply. Neglects lead and brush resistance and thermal limits.

name: Gripper Grasp Force (Friction Grasp)
description: Computes the minimum normal force each finger of a robotic gripper must apply to hold an object by friction. It balances the total inertial load m×(g+a) against the available friction from n fingers with coefficient mu.
notes: The acceleration a accounts for motion or shaking beyond gravity; set a=0 for a static hold. Result is force per finger. Add a safety factor, as mu is uncertain and slip is catastrophic.

name: Servo Angle from PWM Pulse Width
description: Converts a hobby-servo PWM pulse width into a commanded angle. It maps the 1000–2000 microsecond range linearly onto 0–180 degrees, so a 1500 microsecond pulse corresponds to 90 degrees.
notes: Assumes the common 1000–2000 us convention and a 180-degree servo; many servos use 500–2500 us or different sweeps, which shifts the mapping. Pulse width is in microseconds.

name: Belt Drive Output Speed
description: Finds the rotational speed of the driven pulley in a belt or pulley drive. Assuming no slip, the output speed equals the driver speed scaled by the ratio of driver to driven pulley diameters, n1×D1/D2.
notes: Assumes no belt slip and constant belt length. D1 and D2 must share the same unit, which then cancels; only their ratio matters. Larger driven pulley reduces speed and increases torque.

name: Mobile Robot Wheel Slip Ratio
description: Measures the longitudinal slip of a driven wheel during acceleration. It compares the wheel's peripheral speed w×rw with the actual ground speed v, giving the fraction of wheel motion lost to slip, (w×rw − v)/(w×rw).
notes: This driving-slip definition normalises by wheel speed and gives 0 for no slip, near 1 for a spinning wheel. For braking, a different denominator (ground speed) is normally used. Dimensionless ratio.

name: Mobile Robot Battery Runtime
description: Gives a first-order estimate of how long a battery lasts by dividing its charge capacity in amp-hours by the average current draw in amps, yielding runtime in hours.
notes: Ignores usable-capacity limits, voltage sag, Peukert effect and varying loads, so real runtime is shorter. Apply a depth-of-discharge factor for the true available capacity.

name: Lidar Angular Resolution
description: Computes the angular spacing between consecutive lidar measurements. It divides the total field of view by the number of points per scan, giving the angle in degrees between adjacent range readings.
notes: Field of view and result are in degrees; smaller values mean finer angular detail. For a full 360-degree scan, the endpoints coincide, so points effectively partition the circle evenly.

name: Accelerometer Tilt Angle (Single-Axis)
description: Estimates a single-axis tilt angle from an accelerometer reading, theta = asin(ax/g), the angle between that sensor axis and horizontal, assuming the sensor measures only the static gravity component along that axis.
notes: Valid only while the sensor is stationary or moving at constant velocity, since any dynamic acceleration adds error. ax must not exceed g in magnitude, or the arcsine is undefined.
